title: Family
goal: Name family members, explain relationships with *ni* and *kay*, and understand why birth order matters so much in the Philippines.
bekal: name members of the immediate and extended family
explain relationships: *kapatid ni Ana*, *anak nina Ben at Lisa*

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Ilan kayong magkakapatid?

notes: **Magkakapatid means "siblings"** — the prefix *magka-* (and its plural form *magkaka-*) makes words expressing a mutual relationship. Cousins: *magkaibigan* (friends with each other), *magkasama* (together), *mag-asawa* (married couple), *mag-ina* (mother and child).

**Panganay and bunso carry social weight.** The eldest child is expected to be responsible for younger siblings, often well into adulthood; the youngest is pampered and still called *bunso* at forty. Calling yourself *panganay* in the Philippines tells your listener a lot at once.

**Kapatid doesn't distinguish gender** — the word covers both brothers and sisters. When needed: *kapatid na babae* (sister), *kapatid na lalaki* (brother). What does matter is **age**, through the forms of address *ate* and *kuya*.

**Ate and kuya must be used with older siblings.** Calling an older sibling by name alone is considered disrespectful in many Filipino families. The same rule applies to older cousins, and even to older friends.

**Nanay and tatay** are the warmest and most common words for mother and father. There are also *inay/itay* (more intimate), *ina/ama* (standard and a bit formal), and *mama/papa* and *mommy/daddy* used by city families.

**Ang nanay ko naman ay …** uses *naman* as a contrast marker: "as for my mother". This is one of the most frequent jobs of *naman* — shifting the spotlight from one person to another without sounding argumentative.

**Miss mo na sila** is perfect Taglish once more: the English word *miss* used as a Tagalog root. The full form is *na-mi-miss mo sila*, and the pure Tagalog form is *nasasabik ka sa kanila* — which almost no one uses.

**Kain pa!** is a command that isn't really a command but hospitality. At a Filipino table, the host will tell you to eat more again and again; refusing once or twice is considered normal and doesn't stop the offers.
**Katulad ni Ana** = "just like Ana". Notice the marker *ni* because the comparison is with a person's name. For things: *katulad ng bahay namin*.

grammars.title: Explaining relationships with ni, kay and nina
body: All family relationships are expressed with the markers you set up in unit 5. The only new thing here is the plural forms.

head: Pattern
Example
Meaning
rows: I went to Ana's (place, with her family).

after: *Kina* has a distinct meaning worth noting: **"to the home/place of so-and-so and their people"**. *Pumunta ako kina Ana* doesn't mean "I went to Ana" but "I went to Ana's place".
To ask about a relationship: *Ano ang relasyon mo kay Ana?* or, more casually, *Ano siya sa iyo?* — "what is she to you?"
Mentioning someone else's parent still uses the respectful marker: *ang nanay **ni** Ana*, not *si nanay ni Ana*.

grammars.title: Family members
body: Notice how many you may already know: *anak*, *asawa*, *biyenan*, *bayaw* all have cousins in Malay.
after: **Ninong and ninang** are a social institution of their own in the Philippines: godparents who have lifelong duties to give gifts, help with school and help the godchild find work. One child can have a dozen or more.
*Kamag-anak* (relatives) contains the word *anak* (child) inside — a structure that's easy to read once you know the root.
The forms *tito* and *tita* are also used with parents' friends who aren't relatives at all, just like "uncle" and "auntie" in many Asian and Philippine English settings.

head: Question
Meaning
Sample answer
rows: Ano ang trabaho ng tatay mo?

blocks.text: Questions about marital status, age and salary are far more ordinary in the Philippines than in most Western settings — and aren't considered impolite. Answering briefly with a smile is enough; you aren't required to explain.

blocks.title: Pamilya isn't just the nuclear family
items: A Filipino household commonly contains three generations plus a cousin studying at college. When someone says *nakatira ako sa bahay namin*, the number of people in it could be ten.
That's why *ate* and *kuya* are used far beyond biological siblings: cousins, neighbors, an older sibling's friend, even a regular driver. The rule isn't blood, it's age.

blocks.text: **OFW** — *Overseas Filipino Worker* — isn't just an abbreviation but one of the most meaningful words in the Philippines. Around ten percent of the population works abroad, and almost every family has one. Asking about it is a natural conversation opener, but remember it often carries a story of long separation.
